statement: Your words “i want to go straight back to it” fit only loosely what the Vedic and yogic texts call Rāga (attachment). Rāga is what follows upon pleasure (YS 2.7). Vyāsa: in one who has known pleasure, preceded by the memory of pleasure, the greed, thirst and craving (gardha, tṛṣṇā, lobha) for pleasure or for its means — that is rāga.

statement: Each names a false or inflated 'I'. YS: I-am-ness is the seeming identity of the power of the seer and the power of seeing (YS 2.6). Vyāsa: the puruṣa is the seer's power, the buddhi the power of seeing (YB 2.6). Gītā: arrogance and conceit (darpa, abhimāna) belong to the demonic endowment (BhG 16.4), which leads to bondage (BhG 16.5). TS: pride (māna) is one of the four passions (TS 8.9), by which the soul takes in karmic matter (TS 8.2). Visuddhimagga: personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) regards form and the other aggregates as self (Vism XVII) and is one of the five lower fetters; conceit (māna) is a defilement and a fetter that remains until the arahat path (Vism XXII). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity.

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original: daivī sampadvimokṣāya nibandhāyāsurī matā|mā śucaḥ sampadaṃ daivīmabhijāto'si pāṇḍava
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: the divine endowment is held to lead to release (vimokṣa), the demonic to bondage (nibandha). Do not grieve (mā śucaḥ), Pāṇḍava: you are born to the divine endowment.

statement: Asmitā is not pride. YS 2.6 names a confusion of the seer with its instrument, a structural error that is present even without any haughtiness. The Gītā's darpa and abhimāna and the Jain māna are attitudes of self-exaltation: the Gītā lists them among the marks of a bad endowment (BhG 16.4), and TS grades māna in four intensities (TS 8.9). They meet only in the 'I'. Personality view comes closest to asmitā, since both take something that is not the self as the self. The Yoga also counts that as an error (YS 2.5), but it corrects the error by isolating a real seer (YS 2.25). The Visuddhimagga's remedy is to abandon the view, which is one of the five lower fetters, and conceit remains until the arahat path (Vism XXII). It does not isolate a seer in the view's place. Whether a seer remains is not yet reconciled (row ot:provisional-self-question of one_truth.json).

cite.paraphrase: From the absence of that (ignorance), the conjunction is absent; this is the abandonment (hāna), the seer's isolation (kaivalya).

cite.paraphrase: On "with five factors abandoned": the abandoned factors are the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa): sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill will (vyāpāda), sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha), restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) and doubt (vicikicchā). Though other unwholesome states are also abandoned at the moment of jhāna, these five in particular are the obstructions to jhāna. Harmed by doubt it does not climb the way that leads to attaining the jhāna.

cite.paraphrase: The five lower fetters are personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rites and observances, sensual lust and ill will (paṭigha), which bind to lower aggregates and the like. Defilements (kilesa), being themselves defiled and defiling their associated states, are ten: greed, hate, delusion, conceit, view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing. Wrongnesses (micchatta) are eight: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration, or ten with wrong release and wrong knowledge. Worldly conditions (lokadhamma) are eight: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain, blame and praise; here the text says liking for what is gained and resentment for what is not gained are taken under those. Avarice (macchariya) is fivefold: over dwelling, family, gain, teaching and praise. Perversions (vipallāsa) are three: of perception, of mind and of view, taking the impermanent, painful, not-self and unlovely as permanent, pleasant, self and beautiful. Ties (gantha) are four: covetousness, ill will, adherence to rites and observances, and the insistence that "this alone is truth". Wrong courses (agati) are doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done through desire, hate, delusion and fear. Taints (āsava) is a name for sensual lust, lust for existence, wrong view and ignorance, so called because they flow out (as far as change-of-lineage and the top of existence by way of object, or through the unguarded doors like water through the holes of a jar, in the sense of constant trickling), or because they make the suffering of the round flow (continued on p. 684).

cite.paraphrase: The five lower fetters are personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rites and observances, sensual lust and ill will (paṭigha), which bind to lower aggregates and the like. Defilements (kilesa), being themselves defiled and defiling their associated states, are ten: greed, hate, delusion, conceit, view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing. Wrongnesses (micchatta) are eight: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration, or ten with wrong release and wrong knowledge. Worldly conditions (lokadhamma) are eight: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain, blame and praise; here the text says liking for what is gained and resentment for what is not gained are taken under those. Avarice (macchariya) is fivefold: over dwelling, family, gain, teaching and praise. Perversions (vipallāsa) are three: of perception, of mind and of view, taking the impermanent, painful, not-self and unlovely as permanent, pleasant, self and beautiful. Ties (gantha) are four: covetousness, ill will, adherence to rites and observances, and the insistence that "this alone is truth". Wrong courses (agati) are doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done through desire, hate, delusion and fear. Taints (āsava) is a name for sensual lust, lust for existence, wrong view and ignorance, so called because they flow out (as far as change-of-lineage and the top of existence by way of object, or through the unguarded doors like water through the holes of a jar, in the sense of constant trickling), or because they make the suffering of the round flow (continued on p. 684).

cite.paraphrase: Concluding the imperfections: he regards illumination, knowledge and the rest as "this is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self", and so regarding does not waver or tremble at them. The ancients say: one whose understanding is practised in these ten spots is skilled in restlessness about the Dhamma and is not distracted. So not distracted, he unpicks the thirty-fold tangle of imperfections and defines the path and the not-path: illumination and the rest are not the path; the insight-knowledge that has entered the true course, free of imperfections, is the path. The knowledge that stands, knowing the path and the not-path, is the purification by knowledge and vision of what is path and not-path. At this point he has defined the three truths: by defining mind-and-matter in the purification of view he has defined suffering; by discerning conditions in the purification by overcoming doubt, the origin; by determining the right path here, the path. The chapter ends with the colophon, the twentieth chapter.

cite.paraphrase: Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is that by which one sees wrongly, or which sees wrongly, or mere wrong seeing: its mark is unwise insistence; its function is clinging; its manifestation is wrong adherence; its proximate cause is the wish not to see the noble ones and the like; it is to be regarded as the most blameworthy. Restlessness (uddhacca) is agitated state: its mark is non-calming; its function is unsteadiness, like water stirred by wind; its manifestation is bewilderment, like a flag fluttering in the wind or like ashes thrown up by a blow on a stone; its proximate cause is unwise attention to the non-calming of the mind; it is to be regarded as distraction of consciousness. The other factors are as stated for the unwholesome. The second unwholesome consciousness is like the first, but prompted and with sloth-torpor indeterminate. Sloth (thīna) is the sinking, torpor (middha) the drowsing: sloth has as its mark lack of energy and as function dispelling energy, as manifestation sinking; torpor has as mark unworkableness, as function smothering, as manifestation drooping or drowsy sleep; for both the proximate cause is unwise attention to discontent, lazy stretching and the like. Conceit (māna), indeterminate in the third and fourth, has as mark haughtiness, as function self-promotion, as manifestation vain-glory, as proximate cause greed dissociated from view; it is to be regarded as madness. The fifth to eighth are given in the same manner without wrong view or with joy left out.

statement: Rāga is not kāmacchanda, and neither is lobha. (1) Framework: YS rāga is one of five kleśas growing in the field of avidyā (YS 2.4). The Gītā's kāma is born of the guṇa rajas and is one enemy with anger (BhG 3.37). Kāmacchanda is a hindrance: a state to be noticed and abandoned in meditation (MN 10:36). Taṇhā is the origin of suffering (DN 22:19). Jain lobha is a passion-felt deluding karma (kaṣāya-vedanīya, TS 8.9) and a literal cause of karmic matter binding the soul (TS 8.2). (2) Scope: YS rāga covers any remembered pleasure and its means (YB 2.7). Kāmacchanda is sensual desire. Taṇhā in DN 22 also includes craving for being and for non-being (DN 22:19); the Yoga puts the wish to go on being under a different kleśa (abhiniveśa, YS 2.9). Jain lobha comes in four intensities, anantānubandhī to saṃjvalana (TS 8.9), a grading no other lens uses. The Theravāda lists grade it differently, by depth: a hindrance that keeps jhāna from arising (Vism IV), greed as a root of unwholesome consciousness (Vism XIV), and sensual lust as one of the five lower fetters (Vism XXII). (3) What is freed: the Yoga ends in the seer's aloneness (YS 2.25), the suttas in the cessation of craving (DN 22:20), the Jain path in the soul's release from karmic matter (TS 8.2). The self-question behind these three ends is not yet reconciled (row ot:provisional-self-question in one_truth.json).

cite.original: 4.3. Dhammānupassanāāyatanapabba Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhuñca pajānāti, rūpe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Sotañca pajānāti, sadde ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Ghānañca pajānāti, gandhe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Jivhañca pajānāti, rase ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Kāyañca pajānāti, phoṭṭhabbe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Manañca pajānāti, dhamme ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.
cite.paraphrase: Contemplation of dhammas, third section: the six internal and external sense bases (āyatana). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating dhammas with regard to them. Here a monk knows the eye and knows forms, and he knows the fetter (saṁyojana) that arises dependent on both; he knows how an unarisen fetter comes to arise, how an arisen fetter is abandoned, and how an abandoned fetter will not arise again in the future. He does the same for the ear and sounds, the nose and smells, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and dhammas.

statement: On the sense of 'I': Jain, Yoga, Upaniṣadic and Buddhist texts all teach that one is not the body, nor any passing state of mind. The Yoga Sūtra calls the seer's seeming oneness with the mind 'I-am-ness'; Theravāda texts teach seeing 'this is not mine, I am not this'. They differ on what is left: Jain texts, many souls whose changing states are their own; the Yoga Sūtra, many seers that never change; the Upaniṣads, a self that is brahman; Theravāda texts, nothing that is a self. These are different answers, not one.

cite.paraphrase: The seer is seeing alone (dṛśi-mātra); though pure, it looks on cognitions (pratyaya).

statement: Read through the Buddhist texts, your words “i want to go straight back to it” come closest to what they call Kāmacchanda (sensual desire) (a partial match for Rāga (attachment)). Contemplating dhammas as the five hindrances: when sensual desire is present in him the monk knows 'there is sensual desire in me'; when absent, 'there is no sensual desire in me'; he knows how the unarisen sensual desire arises, how the arisen sensual desire is abandoned, and how the abandoned sensual desire does not arise again.

cite.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
cite.original: 4. Dhammānupassanā 4.1. Dhammānupassanānīvaraṇapabba Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa kāmacchandassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa kāmacchandassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa byāpādassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa byāpādassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa byāpādassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa thinamiddhassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa thinamiddhassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa uddhaccakukkuccassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ vicikicchaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ vicikicchaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannāya vicikicchāya uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannāya vicikicchāya pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnāya vicikicchāya āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.
cite.paraphrase: Contemplation of dhammas, first section: the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating dhammas in dhammas with regard to the five hindrances. Here, when sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is present in him he knows 'there is sensual desire in me'; when it is absent he knows 'there is no sensual desire in me'; he knows how unarisen sensual desire comes to arise; he knows how arisen sensual desire is abandoned; and he knows how the abandoned sensual desire will not arise again in the future. He does the same, in exactly this fivefold way, for ill will (byāpāda), for dullness and drowsiness (thina-middha), for restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) and for doubt (vicikicchā).
